# The Cost of Intelligence, Episode 23: Gemini and GPT Tied on the Test, and One Costs 61% More


### Same score, different bill: Throughput Thursday prices AI by the finished task. Plus the selloff that clawed back, Dell’s record quarter, bets on GPU rent, and a $1,750 bot moved to a desk box.


[Strong Compute](https://substack.com/@strongcompute)


Nov 26, 2026


*Listen to this episode on [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/0mki7wG0UmGlS3lNJZjZsc) or watch it on [YouTube](https://youtu.be/mNOtAb1dIt0) .*


Welcome back to


**The Cost of Intelligence** , our comedy news show about the money behind AI. Each episode, Ben Sand reads the industry’s invoice and asks one question: are you getting more intelligence per dollar?


Happy Thanksgiving. This week:


**Throughput Thursday** prices AI by the finished task, not the token.


**The AI selloff** came back Wednesday morning, then the market clawed most of it back, taking


**Dell** and


**Anthropic** along for the ride.


**Polymarket** now takes bets on GPU rent.


**Harvey** made an open-weight model better at legal work on fewer tokens. Plus three cuts from the Department of Token Efficiency. Here’s the written version, with every source linked.


---


## Throughput Thursday


Once a week, we ask what a dollar of AI actually gets done. We measure it in dollars per task: the lower the price per task, the more work your dollar buys. Our scoreboard is


[Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/leaderboards/models) , an independent tester: same tests for every model, coding to science, then the bill per task.


**The two ends.** The priciest task on our board: Anthropic’s


**Claude Fable 5.2** on max, with the top score,


**65** , at about


**$26.50 a task** . At the other end, some small models cost


**under 15 cents** a task.


**A dead heat at 62.** Google’s


**Gemini 4 Neon** on extra-high ties OpenAI’s


**GPT-6.2 Astra** on max. Same score. On Astra, a task costs


**$4.00** . On Neon,


**$6.44** . That’s


**61% more** for the exact same grade.


**The bargain is still the bargain.** OpenAI’s


**GPT-6.2 Sol** on max scores


**57** for about


**$1 a task** . Anthropic’s


**Claude Opus 5.5** on max beats it by two points, at about


**$10 a task** . Two more points for ten times the money.


**Cheaper tokens, pricier tasks.** Google’s


**Gemini 4 Carbon** charges a quarter of Astra’s token price (


[Google’s pricing](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/pricing) ), but it burns far more tokens on each task, so a task costs


**$7.76** : nearly double Astra. And


**Gemini 4 Argon** costs about


**$10 a task** on this test. On


**December 1** , Google doubles Argon’s price (Carbon’s goes up that day too).


**The chips.** SemiAnalysis ran an agentic inference test: the long sessions a coding agent runs. Amazon’s first


**Trainium3** results came in at roughly


**twice** the performance per dollar of Nvidia’s GB300 (2.28x in


[SemiAnalysis’s post](https://x.com/SemiAnalysis_/status/2125658708357128703) ). That’s on SemiAnalysis’s own cost estimates, for one model, and it’s an early preview Amazon submitted itself. Wait for the rematch.


**The real world.** Atlassian tracked AI spend per unit of shipped code (a merged pull request, weighted by size) at nearly


**500 companies** . In April that AI cost was about


**$9** . By September it was about


**$40** : four and a half times as much. October came in


**27% lower** , but Atlassian says one month is too early to call a trend, and it calls its numbers a floor. In its monthly survey,


**40%** of knowledge workers said they’d been asked to monitor or justify their AI use, hit a cap, lost access, or been moved to a cheaper tool (


[Atlassian](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/company-news/introducing-the-atlassian-ai-sdlc-index) ).


All that to drive a future filled with


**Sous-chef Intelligence** : the big model calls the shots, and a small one chops the onions.


*Per-dollar verdict: don’t judge the meal by the menu. Judge it by the check.*


---


## The big stories


**The selloff came back, then clawed back.** On Wednesday, the last trading day before Thanksgiving, the Nasdaq was down more than


**4.5%** at its worst and closed down about


**0.6%** . Reuters reported the Nasdaq 100 briefly sat


**20%** below its record close from early October. Nvidia fell as much as


**9%** and closed down about


**3.9%** ; memory and neocloud stocks fell too. The new ingredient: proposed US tariffs on


**14** trading partners, including Taiwan, Korea and Japan, with hotter inflation data piling on (


[Reuters, via Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/nasdaq-futures-slide-over-2-on-fresh-us-tariff-concerns-inflation-data-in-focus-5050138) ).


**Dell.** Dell’s sales more than doubled last quarter to about


**$55 billion** . AI servers alone were about


**$22 billion** , almost four times a year ago. Dell now expects about


**$202 billion** in sales this fiscal year, up about


**78%** (


[Dell’s results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001571996/000157199626000050/exhibit991earnings8kq3fy27.htm) ). The stock fell as much as


**10%** on Wednesday, then closed up about 0.6%.


**Anthropic, the IPO that won’t sit still.** On Tuesday it closed below its


**$83** IPO price for the first time, at $81.91. Wednesday morning it sank to about


**$74** . By early afternoon it was back above $83. It still closed below, at $82.79 (


[CNBC on the post-IPO stock](https://www.cnbc.com/investingclub/2026/11/25/anthropics-stock-has-been-a-clunker-post-ipo-why-that-matters-for-the-ai-trade.html) ).


*Per-dollar verdict: the stock prices move every minute. Your API price hasn’t moved.*


**Betting on the chips themselves.** Polymarket now takes bets on what Nvidia’s


**H100, B200 and B300** will rent for, out to


**2028** . CEO Shayne Coplan calls it “a yield curve for the cost of compute”. The December H100 market traded about


**$380,000** on its first day (


[The State of AI](https://thestateofai.com/news/polymarket-wall-street-ai-compute) ).


**Fewer tokens for the lawyers.** Harvey makes AI software for lawyers. With Baseten, it post-trained four new American open-weight models on its legal recipe. The best was Meta’s


**Muse Spark Open** : on Legal Agent Bench it passed every check on


**30.3%** of tasks, against


**25.8%** for the original model on maximum effort. And the trained model wrote


**36% fewer** output tokens per task (


[Harvey](https://www.harvey.ai/blog/applying-the-harvey-tenet-training-recipe-to-us-open-weight-models) ). More tasks finished on fewer tokens means a cheaper finished task.


**The fine print:** Harvey’s own test, and no dollar prices. Output tokens are only part of the bill.


---


## The Department of Token Efficiency


**Cut one: Coder.** Coder makes software for running coding agents. It routes every agent request through its own AI gateway: when its desk boxes are free, jobs go to open models on them; when they’re busy, it falls back to Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet. Product manager


**Ben Potter** wrote it up. One documentation-check bot reviews 50 to 100 code changes a day. On Claude Opus it cost about


**$1,750 a month** . Now it runs on one desk box for a little under


**$11 a month** , mostly electricity. The box cost


**$8,000** , and Potter says this one job pays it off in a little over four months. One problem: the small model kept failing until Potter rewrote the prompt by hand (


[Coder](https://coder.com/blog/running-open-weight-models-at-coder) ).


**The fine print:** one workflow. The boxes are slower than Sonnet, so background jobs only. Coder sells the gateway, and its first box was a free demo unit from Nvidia and Dell. The bot saves about


**$21,000 a year** (our math); Coder says its whole AI bill is heading for


**$5 million** this year.


**Cut two: Delegent.** Researchers at the University of Waterloo built it. Delegent runs on Claude Code: the frontier model stays in charge, and the grunt work (finding code, running tests, searching) goes to a small model on your own hardware. On 50 long coding tasks, OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol working alone ran up about


**$2.10 a task** in frontier fees. With a small helper, about


**70 cents** . Same number of tasks solved (


[the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33098) ).


**The fine print:** it’s a research paper, and nobody got an invoice. The cost of running the small model on your own machine isn’t counted. And it’s slower: the typical task took 38 minutes, against 25 for the big model alone.


**Cut three: Qoder.** Qoder makes an AI coding tool. It found some requests were missing the cache, the discount for reusing work the model already did. So it put the shared instructions first, and sent each chat back to the server that already had its work. Qoder says the average task used to cost


**4.4 credits** ; now it’s


**2.6** . So the same quota covers about


**17 tasks instead of 10** (


[Qoder](https://blog.qoder.com/qoder-auto-cache-optimization) ).


**The fine print:** these are Qoder’s own numbers, in its credits, not dollars. The models behind its Auto mode change over time.
